title: Negative SEO: attack types, why they rarely work now, and how to defend your site
summary: Jacky Chou explains what negative SEO is, the main attack types (link farms, fake link-removal requests, hacking, heavy crawling, duplicate content, fake reviews), and why Google's Penguin 4.0 makes link-spam attacks far less effective. He gives a monitoring and defense checklist: traffic and Search Console alerts, backlink audits, disavowing, securing admin logins, and site speed.

principles.text: Negative SEO works far less than it used to, but it isn't zero risk; monitor rather than assume Google handles it.
principles.quote: While negative SEO can still work, it is far less of an issue than it was some years back.

principles.text: Google now devalues link spam instead of penalizing whole sites, so link-farm attacks mostly fail.
principles.quote: Rather than devaluing whole websites, Google now devalues link spam.

principles.text: Defending against negative SEO means watching your whole online presence, not just backlinks.
principles.quote: It is now necessary to monitor your complete online presence and implement good security measures to keep negative SEO attacks at bay.

principles.text: Detect attacks early by tracking organic traffic and Google's notifications; faster detection means less damage.
principles.quote: The sooner you learn about the negative SEO, the sooner you can respond and mitigate the harm.

principles.text: Audit your backlink profile regularly and keep your disavow file updated for toxic links you can't remove.
principles.quote: If you receive fresh harmful backlinks that you cannot delete, update your disavow file regularly.

principles.text: Harden admin access and run regular site audits so hackers can't inject spam, alter redirects or robots.txt.
principles.quote: Hackers usually need administrator access to interfere with your site, and by adding extra layers of protection, you can substantially minimize the chances that they'll be able to break in.
